claims.text: Single-phase formation in noble-metal-based HEA nanoparticles is governed by kinetic trapping during rapid heating and cooling.
An ultrashort high-temperature dwell causes simultaneous precursor decomposition.
An ultrashort high-temperature dwell limits atomic diffusion.
Limited diffusion during rapid processing freezes a homogenized elemental distribution into a metastable single-phase solid solution.
Increasing the high-temperature dwell time increases atomic mobility sufficiently for thermodynamic driving forces to act.
The increased mobility produced by a longer dwell promotes phase separation and elemental segregation.
Before flash processing, the constituent elements are uniformly distributed at the nanoscale in the supported precursor or pre-alloyed nanoparticle state.
The controlled intervention is to vary only the peak-temperature dwell time while maintaining rapid heating and cooling rates.
The proposed processing regime uses heating rates of about 10^5 K/s, a peak temperature of about 2000 K, and cooling rates of about 10^4–10^5 K/s under inert or reductive atmospheres.
Support-material nucleation sites aid formation of the kinetically trapped atomic arrangement.
Ultrafast heating decomposes the precursors and creates liquid droplets.
The liquid droplets contain a well-mixed multimetallic solution.
Rapid cooling freezes the mixed droplet state before significant atomic migration occurs.
Under the ultrashort-dwell baseline, the nanoparticles will have a homogeneous single-phase FCC or other targeted crystal structure with uniform elemental distribution.
Increasing dwell time will produce detectable phase separation.
Increasing dwell time will produce detectable elemental segregation.
Increasing dwell time may produce coarser particle morphology.
Established rapid-shock or carbothermal methods with sub-100 ms dwell times produce single-phase, uniformly mixed HEA nanoparticles approximately 5–12 nm in size.
The hypothesis is intended to apply to noble-metal systems containing at least five elements processed with extreme heating and cooling rates.
The hypothesis may not apply to solution-based, prolonged-thermal, or low-energy synthesis routes because their diffusion limitations differ.
